benchmarks.name: RepairPal
benchmarks.note: national average, all vehicles: parts about $749 plus labor $150-$219, before taxes and fees; page says estimates last updated September 3, 2026. The page does not say whether this is one caliper or both on an axle, and says the pads (and rotors if needed) must also be replaced. ONLY benchmark loaded: the run's shared web-search limit was reached before a second and third could be found

finding: The live range of $170-$825 looks about right for one front caliper, but this check is incomplete and should be treated as provisional. Built totals for one front caliper, parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks), with no fluid bleed charge, pads or core charge: midsize 2015 Hyundai Sonata about $206-$496 (0.8-1.0 hr); truck/SUV 2016 Dodge Durango about $166-$337 (0.6-1.0 hr); luxury 2017 Cadillac XT5 about $212-$331 (1.0 hr), plus a $40 core charge if the old caliper is not returned; economy 2015 Toyota Corolla: upper end about $441 ($280.92 Toyota list price + 1.0 hr), lower end not built because no aftermarket price could be loaded. The bottom: our lowest total is about $166 (a $94 aftermarket caliper with bracket and a 0.6-hour warranty time), so $170 is a fair floor; a real quote will usually be higher because it adds brake fluid and bleeding. The top: the dearest caliper we priced for the basic Sonata gives about $496, and the larger-brake Sonata calipers on the same Hyundai catalog page list at $516-$563, which with 1.0 hr comes to about $680-$725, so $825 leaves reasonable room for a bleed and a pricier vehicle. We did not price a European luxury car or a multi-piston performance caliper, which can cost far more than anything here. RepairPal's national average of $898-$968 sits above the live top; it assumes about $749 in parts, several times the list price of any single caliper we found, and the page does not say whether it covers one caliper or an axle, so it does not by itself show that the live top is too low. How solid the labor times are: all four are manufacturer warranty times from recall bulletins, which is good, but warranty times are the low end of what shops bill. Midsize (0.8 hr), truck/SUV (0.6 hr) and luxury (1.0 hr) are for the example vehicle itself; economy is a Mazda3 time (0.6 hr), not a Corolla. The upper end of 1.0 hr for economy, midsize and truck is the GM time for a different vehicle. Only one bulletin (2015 Chevrolet Colorado, both front calipers, 1.2 hr) says the time includes bleeding the brakes; the others do not say. What is missing: an aftermarket or remanufactured price for the Corolla and the XT5 (the XT5 low end is a discounted genuine part), a second parts source for the Corolla, a stated time for a half-ton pickup, and two more benchmarks. The run's shared web-search limit was reached before these could be found.
extras: A quote usually adds brake fluid and bleeding the brakes (often charged as a brake fluid service). Many shops replace calipers in pairs on the same axle, which roughly doubles the parts and adds less than double the labor (manufacturer bulletins allow 0.7-1.4 hr for both fronts against 0.6-1.0 hr for one). Also common: new brake pads on that axle (a leaking or seized caliper often ruins them; the bulletins add 0.1-0.2 hr), rotors if they are scored or overheated, a new brake hose, a caliper bracket and hardware when the caliper is sold without them, a core charge that is refunded when the old caliper is returned (remanufactured and some genuine calipers; $40 on the Cadillac part), a brake inspection or diagnosis fee, shop supplies and sales tax. Rear calipers with a built-in parking brake, electric parking brakes and multi-piston performance calipers cost more.
